extracted.intended_audience: attorneys practicing before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office; OED counsel; disciplinary adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, evidentiary burdens, rule citations, aggravating/mitigating factors, and sanctioning procedures applied in USPTO disciplinary proceedings against practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for PTO discipline (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D), 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress authorized the PTO to promulgate regulations governing 'the recognition and conduct of agents, attorneys, or other persons representing applicants or other parties before the Office.' 35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2)(D). If an attorney does not comply with regulations issued under §2(b)(2)(D), or is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' the PTO may suspend or exclude the attorney from further practice before the PTO. 35 U.S.C. §32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admission and to suspend or exclude practitioners. These statutes provide the legal basis for disciplinary proceedings and for imposing sanctions such as suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101-11.901)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO issued revised regulations governing attorney conduct titled 'Rules of Professional Conduct' codified at 37 C.F.R. §§11.101-11.901.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rules are based upon the ABA Model Rules. In interpreting and applying the PTO Rules, the PTO looks to the PTO Code (prior rules), Comments and Annotations to the ABA Model Rules, and decisions/opinions issued by state bars. The Rules provide the substantive obligations (e.g., diligence, communication, recordkeeping) alleged to be violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. §11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must prove alleged violations by 'clear and convincing evidence.' Likewise, a respondent must prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. This standard falls between a preponderance of the evidence and proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined in the decision as requiring evidence that produces 'a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy' as to the truth of the allegations. 'Evidence is clear if it is certain, unambiguous, and plain to the understanding, and it is convincing if it is reasonable and persuasive enough to cause the trier of facts to believe it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to act with reasonable diligence (37 C.F.R. §11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.103 requires practitioners to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client. The Complaint alleged violations relating primarily to the quality and timeliness of legal services provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failing this obligation include repeated unfulfilled promises to deliver drafts, extended non-responsiveness to client inquiries, missed or delayed filings, and representations about work completion that are not met. Such conduct may support a finding of violation when proven by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to keep the client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. §11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.104(a)(3) obligates practitioners to keep clients reasonably informed about the status of their matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner communications lapses—failure to reply to client emails/phone calls, failing to provide drafts or status updates—are evidence of violating this rule. The decision treats frequent unanswered inquiries and long gaps in communication as support for this violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with OED / respond to lawful demands (37 C.F.R. §11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.801(b) requires practitioners to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) and not knowingly fail to respond to lawful demands for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays or intentional non-responsiveness to OED Requests for Information (RFIs) or other investigatory demands are treated as violations. The decision distinguishes between bad-faith obstruction and organizational dysfunction but finds failure to cooperate is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. §11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.804(d) prohibits conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that undermines the client relationship, the disciplinary process, or the integrity of proceedings can fall under this provision. The Director alleged and the Tribunal found conduct falling within this rule based on the pattern of delays, misrepresentations to the client, and recordkeeping failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping — failure to keep separate client account funds (37 C.F.R. §11.115(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.115(a) requires practitioners to keep client funds separate from the practitioner's own property and to have a separate and identifiable account for client funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must maintain separate client trust accounts and preserve records relating to client funds; failure to do so (including commingling or lack of a separate account) constitutes a rule violation. The decision notes a five-year retention expectation for certain records after termination of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping — failure to keep complete financial records (37 C.F.R. §11.115(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.115(f)(1) requires practitioners to maintain complete financial records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of noncompliance include patchy bookkeeping, missing bank records, and failure to preserve client trust ledgers. Such deficiencies support disciplinary findings where the required records are absent or incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA Standards, Rules 9.22, 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards identify numerous aggravating factors to be considered in sanction assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision lists and applies aggravators including: substantial experience in the practice of law; evidence of a pattern of misconduct (including prior warning letters); refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct; and multiple offenses. These increase the severity of sanctions. The Tribunal considered the Director's recommended two-year suspension but weighed aggravating factors in selecting an appropriate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA Standards Rule 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards identify mitigating factors relevant to penalty determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision recognizes mitigating factors such as: absence of a prior disciplinary record; violative actions stemming from a good-faith effort to help a friend (no dishonest/selfish motive); vulnerability or provocation by the client; and evidence of personal/organizational problems (executive functioning deficits) that impacted performance. Mitigators reduce severity of sanctions and can support stayed suspensions and probation instead of outright suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning principles — proportionality, protection of the public, and deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions should be proportionate to the violation, aim to protect the public and the profession, and serve as deterrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal explicitly considers proportionality (penalty should fit the violation), the need to protect the public and the Bar, and deterrence as primary sentencing objectives. The decision weighs these factors against aggravating/mitigating circumstances to craft appropriate sanctions (e.g., stayed suspension with probation and conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of actual harm to client intellectual property rights (AIA/35 U.S.C. §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing damages or prejudice, the Tribunal considers whether practitioner conduct caused loss of patent rights, including under the AIA first-inventor-to-file and 35 U.S.C. §102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision requires evidentiary support that delays or misconduct led to actual harm (e.g., another filing that defeated client's rights). Mere potential loss is insufficient without evidence of a filed application or other concrete harm; short delays may not establish compensable loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior warnings and prior discipline as evidence of a pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior communications from OED (e.g., warning letters) or earlier discipline can be considered as evidence of a pattern of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior warning about obligations (such as acting with reasonable diligence and keeping clients informed) is an aggravating factor that suggests an inclination toward rule violations even if not a formal disciplinary sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural compliance and responsiveness as adjudicative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's procedural behavior in the disciplinary process—timeliness of answers, filing prehearing statements, responses to motions, attendance and preparedness at hearing—are relevant to the Tribunal's assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures such as submitting only a partial answer, filing an amended answer late, not filing a prehearing statement, not responding to motions for summary judgment, appearing late to hearing, and failing to assert defenses are viewed negatively and may reflect organizational problems or lack of respect for proceedings, affecting sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for finding bad-faith obstruction of disciplinary process
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad-faith obstruction (an aggravating factor) involves intentional failure to comply with rules or orders to hinder the investigation or proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal distinguishes between intentional obstruction and conduct resulting from organizational dysfunction; to find bad-faith obstruction, there must be evidence of intentionality, submission of false evidence, deceitful practices, or deliberate noncompliance with orders. Mere delays or non-responsiveness without evidence of intent may not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards, Model Rules and state bar decisions to interpret obligations and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO relies on ABA Standards, the ABA Model Rules' comments and annotations, the prior PTO Code, and state bar decisions in interpreting the PTO Rules and in considering appropriate sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These authorities provide both substantive interpretive guidance (what conduct violates a rule) and sentencing guidance (what sanctions are typical for particular violations), and are explicitly referenced by the Tribunal in reaching findings and penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for stayed suspension and probation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a suspension is stayed and probation is imposed, the Tribunal may set specific conditions the respondent must satisfy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the conditions included: restitution of $2,000 within 90 days; undergoing, at respondent's expense, a full professional neuropsychological assessment covering executive functioning and initiating recommended treatment within 30 days of results; not committing further USPTO disciplinary violations during probation; and contemporaneously providing OED with evidence of compliance. Failure to comply triggers automatic activation of suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedures and timelines (37 C.F.R. §11.55) and duties of suspended practitioners/reinstatement (37 C.F.R. §§11.58, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. §11.55, an appeal of an Initial Decision must be filed within 30 days and must include exceptions and supporting reasons. Rules §11.58 addresses duties of suspended practitioners and §11.60 concerns petitions for reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file a timely appeal constitutes acceptance and waiver of further review. Suspended practitioners have specified duties to follow while suspended, and reinstatement requires compliance with regulatory procedures.
